### 3. Strongest Reason the Outcome Might Fail
Even during intense weeks of the conflict, attacks are episodic and often clustered (e.g., three tankers from the same owner targeted within 17 minutes on 22 November, followed by zero qualifying kinetic incidents occurring on 23 November and 24 November). Furthermore, as UKMTO acknowledged in its recent overviews, many vessels transit with AIS off or do not report incidents directly to UKMTO, or reports cannot be independently verified by UKMTO/JMIC. Thus, a 24-hour window on 28 November could easily pass either as an operational lull between strike packages or with an incident that goes unreported by UKMTO/JMIC.

Balancing the ~58% monthly base rate against the 71% daily rate over the past week, while accounting for the clustering of strikes and multi-day gaps (such as 23–24 Nov), a probability of 0.62 is appropriate.

The ongoing US-Israel-Iran conflict has produced a high but uneven daily rate of UKMTO/JMIC-verified projectile strikes and close explosions against merchant ships in the specified waters. October saw roughly 35 such attacks (about one per day on average); November had already reached at least 22 by the 22nd and continued with multiple verified hits on the 20th–22nd and 25th. JMIC’s 26 November assessment keeps the Strait of Hormuz at SEVERE and calls deliberate hostile action highly likely, while US-assisted transits remain in the low thirties per day, so targets are still present. That recent empirical frequency of days carrying at least one qualifying reported incident is the base rate (roughly two-thirds). No ceasefire or operational pause is in evidence; IRGC statements on 26 November reaffirm the use of force to pressure shipping. The main downward adjustment is the clear clustering: even inside this elevated period there have been full days (23–24 November, and so far 26 November in primary UKMTO products) with no incident dated to them that meets the criterion.
